Trump Has Other Ideas for a Historic Summit.   Plus, Xinjiang goes from blacklisted to global trade hub, Xi’s purges echo Stalin’s, and Kim Jong Un makes a surprise trip to China     Xi Jinping, Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin CHIP SOMODEVILLA/GETTY IMAGES (2); VYACHESLAV PROKOFYEV/PRESS POOL   Xi Jinping probably can’t believe his luck.

   Less than a month before China hosts the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, Vladimir Putin has proposed an unprecedented meeting with President Trump and Xi that could put the Chinese leader at the center of diplomacy over the war in Ukraine.

   Trump is open to the idea . But there is a hitch: China, the prospective host, hasn’t issued an invitation, people familiar with the situation told me. The obstacle is a fundamental disagreement over what the three leaders would discuss.

   Putin wants to focus on Ukraine. Trump has suggested nuclear-arms control instead, an issue Beijing has long resisted discussing with Washington and Moscow.

   For Xi, the prospect is both tantalizing and fraught. A trilateral summit on Chinese soil would offer a dramatic demonstration of China’s arrival as a superpower on par with the U.S. But if the meeting can’t get past the agenda dispute, the opportunity could evaporate before it begins.

   Beijing has coveted the mediating role but never quite pulled it off, in part because its embrace of Moscow has undermined its credibility as a neutral mediator.

   China floated a peace plan for Ukraine in 2023 that omitted any demand for Russia to withdraw its forces from occupied territories. It went nowhere. Such a summit would go far beyond any position paper. It would put Xi physically at the center of the negotiating table.

   Putin pitched the summit around Ukraine. Trump, however, has pointed to nuclear-arms control as the meeting’s potential focus. A trilateral arms talk between those three nations would be a historic first for a U.S. president. Secretary of State Marco Rubio backed the idea, calling it an opportunity for the three nuclear powers to discuss arms control at the leader level. And that’s where Beijing’s enthusiasm runs into a wall. 

   China has long resisted engaging in nuclear talks because it’s far behind. The U.S. and Russia each possess thousands of nuclear warheads. China has a fraction of that. From Beijing’s perspective, joining arms control negotiations now would essentially lock in the country’s nuclear inferiority. No Chinese leader—certainly not Xi, who has overseen the most significant expansion of China’s nuclear arsenal in its history—is going to sign up for that.

   The nuclear wrangling begins   So Beijing’s likely play, according to Yun Sun, director of the China program at Washington-based Stimson Center, is to push back on the arms control framing and see whether Washington insists. If Trump holds firm on the nuclear issue as the price of admission, the summit could stall before it starts.

   Xi’s state visit to Washington last month offered a preview of that standoff.

   The White House readout of the meeting between Trump and Xi mentioned arms control, but only as a U.S. push rather than an agreed-upon agenda item or mutual commitment. According to its summary of the Sept. 24 meeting, Trump renewed his call for China to join trilateral arms control discussions alongside the U.S. and Russia. Beijing’s official readout completely omitted nuclear arms control.

   There is a scenario in which the agenda question resolves itself, Sun said. If a ceasefire or even a framework for ending the Ukraine war starts to take shape in the coming weeks, that “could become the summit’s theme,” she said, “especially given how Beijing would like to portray this summit as the most significant event in the history of world politics since the end of World War II.”

   The irony is that the very dynamics that make such a trilateral appealing to Xi are also the ones that make it risky. 

   A summit that sidelines Ukraine from discussions about its own fate would confirm the worst suspicions of European leaders, many of whom already believe Beijing is comfortable with a protracted war that drains the West while deepening Russia’s dependence on China . It could accelerate the deterioration of China’s relationship with Europe just as Beijing is trying to stave off a trade war with Brussels.

   And then there is Taiwan. If three big powers could get together and talk about Ukraine’s fate, Taipei would wonder: Are we next? But paradoxically, such a summit could also cut against Beijing’s own interests. China has long insisted that Taiwan is a purely internal affair—not something for outside powers to weigh in on. A trilateral summit like this could invite the very outside interference in Taiwan that Xi wants to foreclose.

   Xi’s luck, in other words, comes with a price. The question is whether he thinks it’s worth paying.

   What would you be watching for if this summit actually happens? Write to me at lingling.wei@wsj.com . Include your full name and location, and I might publish your response in an upcoming issue (if you’re reading this in your inbox, you can just hit reply).

   This is an edition of the WSJ China newsletter, a weekly dispatch of exclusive insights on the contest between the U.S. and China, brought to you by the WSJ’s top China correspondent. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here . 

       China in a Few Headlines   • After a five-year review, China approved Citi to set up a wholly owned securities venture in Shanghai offering onshore underwriting and brokerage services.

   • A 16% surge in Chinese aluminum exports has offset Persian Gulf supply disruptions, keeping global prices in check as U.A.E. producers work toward full capacity.

   • China’s third-quarter GDP grew 4.5% on resilient exports , even as deepening property woes and falling investment intensified domestic economic anxiety.

       A Closer Look         Backed by $55 billion in annual state funding and a planned Central Asia railway slated for 2030, Xi Jinping is turning Xinjiang into a trade hub despite global human-rights condemnation.

       Reader Responses   Last week, we asked what Xi’s intensifying purge means for China’s political stability. Readers shared their thoughts: 

   “This purge will lead to Xi being constantly surrounded by yes-men and yes-women. Decision-making will suffer from lack of policy debate. In addition, Xi’s advancing years will leave a leadership vacuum—unless potential successors are publicly visible and empowered. To me this looks like the beginning of a rerun of whatever happened after Mao passed away and the same could happen post-Xi with a different and very unknown cast of characters. Very questionable as to what kind of political stability this can lead to.”— Nipun Ramaiya, U.K. 

   “These widespread purges seem reminiscent of Stalin’s in the 1930s, with a similar potential to be profoundly destabilizing. Stalin was driven by increasing paranoia following his contest with Trotsky and other rivals after Lenin’s death. He was egged on by the murderous Beria, whose power grew in proportion to Stalin’s paranoia.”— John Fitzpatrick, Massachusetts 

   “Xi Jinping’s escalating purge will not deliver genuine political stability to China. Rather than signaling supreme strength, it marks the terminal phase of an authoritarian ‘autoimmune disease,’ wherein a regime that has eliminated all rival factions turns inward to attack its own functional organs, systematically freezing state capacity.”— Shinya Hanamura, Japan 

   (Responses have been condensed and edited.)

This is an edition of the WSJ China newsletter, a weekly dispatch of exclusive insights on the contest between the U.S. and China, brought to you by the WSJ’s top China correspondent. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

China in a Few Headlines

 

• After a five-year review, China approved Citi to set up a wholly owned securities venture in Shanghai offering onshore underwriting and brokerage services.

 

• A 16% surge in Chinese aluminum exports has offset Persian Gulf supply disruptions, keeping global prices in check as U.A.E. producers work toward full capacity.

A Closer Look

 
 
 
 

Backed by $55 billion in annual state funding and a planned Central Asia railway slated for 2030, Xi Jinping is turning Xinjiang into a trade hub despite global human-rights condemnation.

 
 
 

Reader Responses

 

Last week, we asked what Xi’s intensifying purge means for China’s political stability. Readers shared their thoughts:

 

“This purge will lead to Xi being constantly surrounded by yes-men and yes-women. Decision-making will suffer from lack of policy debate. Stalin was driven by increasing paranoia following his contest with Trotsky and other rivals after Lenin’s death. A Name in the News

 
 
North Korea’s official news agency released this image on Oct. 25 showing North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, left, with Wang Huning, a Chinese Communist Party official. KCNA/AFP/GETTY IMAGES
 

Kim Jong Un made a surprise trip to China across a newly opened $300 million border bridge that had sat idle for a decade, meeting senior officials like Wang Huning but not Xi Jinping.
